domains.name: Academic Argumentation
domains.summary: This domain treats argument as the organising purpose of most assessed academic writing and much academic talk: taking a position, supporting claims with evidence and explicit reasoning, anticipating and answering objections, and sequencing sub-claims into a cumulative case. Hirvela (2017) argues that L2 writing pedagogy has given argumentation less attention than its centrality warrants, and Wingate (2012) found that students often receive feedback on 'argument' without being shown what it consists of. Toulmin's model, argumentation schemes and argument mapping are offered as analytical tools rather than templates, and disciplinary variation in what counts as a good argument (Andrews, 2010) is made explicit.
domains.learnerSummary: You will learn what an academic argument is, how to build one from claims, evidence and reasoning, and how to deal fairly and convincingly with other views in writing and in discussion.

stageEmphasis.foundation: Build the concept of argument as a supported position, with simple claim–evidence–explanation links and awareness of how texts persuade.
stageEmphasis.pre-sessional: Develop a sustained, qualified position in source-based essays, with counter-argument, concession and rebuttal, and transfer these moves to seminar discussion.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-ug: Adapt argument to disciplinary genres and evaluate others' arguments in readings, critiques and seminars.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-pgt: Construct extended, evidence-dense arguments in assignments and dissertations, making warrants explicit for expert readers and evaluating research arguments.
stageEmphasis.pgr: Sustain a thesis-length argument, position it within scholarly debates and defend it orally in supervision, conferences and the viva.

domains.name: Critical Thinking
domains.summary: This domain treats critical thinking as a contested, partly discipline-specific set of practices and dispositions — questioning, weighing evidence, recognising inference patterns and their limits, considering perspectives fairly and reflecting on one's own position — that can be made explicit and taught. It deliberately rejects the deficit framing that some groups of learners 'cannot think critically': differences in readiness to critique published work are treated as differences in prior schooling, assessment genres and licence to question, not as cognitive or cultural deficits. The domain supplies the reasoning that the Academic Argumentation domain turns into written and spoken argument.
domains.learnerSummary: You will learn what university tutors mean when they ask you to be 'critical', how to question and weigh evidence and reasoning, and how to notice common errors in thinking — including your own.

stageEmphasis.foundation: Make criticality concrete with familiar topics: description versus analysis, simple questions about evidence, and fair representation of different views.
stageEmphasis.pre-sessional: Connect critical moves to progression tasks — source-based writing, seminars and extended projects — using the course's own criteria and exemplars.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-ug: Embed criticality in disciplinary tasks with module exemplars, especially during the first-year transition when 'be more critical' feedback first appears.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-pgt: Accelerate recalibration to master's-level expectations: evaluating research designs, competing theories and contested literatures from the first assignment.
stageEmphasis.pgr: Focus on evaluating and positioning theory, reflexivity, and the epistemological commitments of one's own research.

domains.name: Identity, Plurilingualism & Intercultural Competence
domains.summary: This domain addresses who learners are as academic language users: how writing and speaking construct identity, how plurilingual repertoires can be used strategically, how English functions as a lingua franca in international universities, and how intercultural and rhetorical differences can be understood without stereotyping. It adopts a resource rather than a deficit orientation, treats culture as dynamic, multiple and partly institutional rather than as fixed national traits, and presents contrastive rhetoric and native-speaker norms as historically influential but contested. Several topics are as much curriculum principles for teachers as content for learners, and are written so that they can serve both.
domains.learnerSummary: You will explore how academic writing and speech shape the way you present yourself, how to use all your languages as resources, and how to communicate confidently across differences without relying on stereotypes.

stageEmphasis.foundation: Build confidence in multilingual repertoires and intercultural group work as learners enter English-medium study, often for the first time.
stageEmphasis.pre-sessional: Address transition, academic identity and explicit conventions alongside lingua franca interaction in multilingual cohorts.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-ug: Support inclusive group work, emerging disciplinary voice and resource-oriented participation for home and international students alike.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-pgt: Help highly international cohorts negotiate identity, intercultural collaboration and unfamiliar expectations within a short programme.
stageEmphasis.pgr: Focus on researcher identity, publishing as a multilingual scholar and positioning within global scholarly communities.

topics.name: What counts as an academic argument
topics.description: Understand an academic argument as a reasoned position on a question, developed through claims supported by evidence and explicit reasoning and responsive to other views — not a quarrel, a one-sided opinion or a well-organised collection of facts. Grasping this reframes most assessed writing as argument and explains feedback such as 'What is your argument?'
masteryEvidence: Distinguishes an argument from a description, a summary and an unsupported opinion when given short texts
States the central argument of a model essay or article in one or two sentences
Identifies the position, the main supporting reasons and any response to other views in a short argumentative text
Explains why an essay with accurate information and clear organisation may still be judged to lack an argument
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner two 150-word paragraphs on the same topic — one an accurate informative summary of research, one taking and supporting a position. Ask which contains an argument and to state that argument in one sentence. Look for recognition that argument requires a contestable position plus support, not just accurate content.

topics.name: Types of claims
topics.description: Distinguish claims of fact (what is the case), definition (what something is or should be classed as), cause (what produces what), value (how good, important or right something is) and policy (what should be done), and recognise that each type calls for different kinds of support. Identifying the claim type an assignment question calls for clarifies what evidence and reasoning the answer needs.
masteryEvidence: Classifies thesis statements and topic sentences by claim type
Identifies the claim type implied by an assignment question (e.g. 'To what extent was X responsible for Y?' as a causal claim)
Specifies the kind of support each claim type typically needs: criteria for value claims, mechanism and design for causal claims, consequences and feasibility for policy claims
Recognises that policy claims usually rest on prior factual, causal and value claims and sequences these in a plan
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give five thesis statements of different types. Ask the learner to classify each and name one piece of evidence or reasoning each would need. Check in particular that value claims are linked to criteria and policy claims to consequences or feasibility.

topics.name: Toulmin model of argument
topics.description: Use Toulmin's model — claim, data or grounds, warrant, backing, qualifier and rebuttal — to analyse how a single argument works and where it is vulnerable. Its value in EAP lies in making visible the usually implicit link (warrant) between evidence and claim and the role of qualification and exceptions, not in providing an essay template.
masteryEvidence: Labels the claim, data, warrant and qualifier in a short academic argument
Articulates an unstated warrant in a sentence of their own
Identifies the rebuttal conditions (exceptions) under which a claim would not hold
Explains how the qualifier reflects the strength of the data and warrant
Shows that the same data can support different claims through different warrants
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give a one-sentence argument with an implicit warrant (e.g. 'Attendance fell after lectures were recorded, so recording lectures reduces attendance'). Ask the learner to supply the warrant, a suitable qualifier and a possible rebuttal. Look for a warrant that states the general principle linking data to claim and a rebuttal that names a specific exception or alternative explanation.

topics.name: Supporting claims
topics.description: Link each claim to evidence and reasoning that are relevant, sufficient and appropriate to the claim's type and strength — drawing on sources, data, examples and explanation — and make clear how each piece of support bears on the claim. This is the basic unit of argumentative writing and speaking, from foundation paragraphs to thesis chapters.
masteryEvidence: Supports each main claim with at least one piece of relevant, attributed evidence
Explains how the evidence supports the claim rather than leaving the connection to the reader
Distinguishes genuine evidence from illustrative examples and hypothetical scenarios and uses each appropriately
Matches the amount and strength of support to the strength of the claim
Identifies and repairs unsupported claims in their own drafts
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner a paragraph containing three claims, only one of which is supported. Ask them to identify the unsupported claims and suggest what kind of evidence each would need. Look for accurate identification and for suggestions that fit the claim type (e.g. comparative data for a claim of increase).

topics.name: Making reasoning explicit
topics.description: State, where readers need it, the reasoning that connects evidence to claim — the principle, mechanism, assumption or criterion that makes the evidence relevant — and support that reasoning when it may be contested. Explicit warrants distinguish analysis from the juxtaposition of facts and claims, especially for readers who do not share the writer's assumptions.
masteryEvidence: Adds an explicit reasoning sentence linking evidence to claim where the link is not obvious to the intended reader
Identifies when a warrant is contestable and provides backing (a source, a mechanism or a principle)
Judges which warrants can be left implicit for an expert disciplinary reader
Uses the language of reasoning accurately (given that, on the assumption that, this suggests that, because)
Detects places in their own drafts where the evidence could equally support a different claim
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give a claim–evidence pair with a debatable warrant (e.g. 'Students rated the new module highly, so it improved their learning'). Ask the learner to write the missing warrant and say whether a sceptical reader would accept it. Look for a warrant that names the assumption (ratings reflect learning) and recognition that it needs backing.

topics.name: Anticipating counter-arguments
topics.description: Identify the strongest objections, alternative explanations and contrary evidence that a knowledgeable reader could raise against one's position, and decide which must be addressed in the text. Anticipating objections is a hallmark of mature argument and of higher-rated student essays, but learners rarely do it spontaneously.
masteryEvidence: Generates at least two substantive objections to their own thesis, including one grounded in evidence rather than opinion
Distinguishes objections to the claim, to the evidence and to the reasoning that links them
Selects the objections most damaging to their position for treatment, rather than the easiest to answer
Locates published sources that express counter-positions
topics.assessmentPrompt: Ask the learner to state the thesis of a current assignment and list the two strongest objections a critical reader could raise, with a source or type of evidence for each. Look for objections that target evidence or reasoning and that the learner finds genuinely challenging, rather than 'some people may disagree' statements.

topics.name: Rebuttal and concession
topics.description: Respond to counter-arguments by conceding what is valid, rebutting what is not with evidence or reasoning, and qualifying one's own position where necessary, using language that acknowledges the other view while keeping the writer's stance dominant. Well-managed concession and rebuttal build credibility and show dialogic engagement with the field.
masteryEvidence: Writes concession–counter sequences (e.g. 'Although X…, Y…') that keep the writer's position dominant
Rebuts an objection with evidence or reasoning rather than simple denial
Qualifies the original claim where a concession warrants it rather than ignoring the concession's implications
Chooses between refutation, partial concession and accommodation according to the strength of the objection
Signals clearly which voice is conceded and which is the writer's own
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner a thesis and one strong objection. Ask for a three-sentence response that concedes part of the objection and maintains a (possibly modified) position. Check for an explicit concession marker, a rebuttal grounded in evidence or reasoning, and a final position consistent with what was conceded.

topics.name: Taking and sustaining a position
topics.description: Commit to a defensible, appropriately qualified position on a question, state it where the genre expects (often in the introduction) and maintain it consistently so that every section of the text contributes to it. A sustained position is what readers and marking criteria most often mean by 'argument' and distinguishes argumentative from merely informative writing.
masteryEvidence: States a clear, specific and contestable position that answers the question set
Calibrates the strength of the position to the evidence available
Maintains the same position from introduction to conclusion, signalling and explaining any qualification
Links each body section explicitly to the position
Reaches a judgement in discussion-type tasks rather than ending with an undecided summary
topics.assessmentPrompt: Ask the learner to read only the introduction, the conclusion and the first sentence of each body paragraph of their own draft, and then state their position. Check whether the position is clear, consistent between introduction and conclusion, and visible at the start of each body section.

topics.name: Structuring an extended argument
topics.description: Sequence sub-claims, evidence and responses to objections into a cumulative case in which each section advances the main position and depends logically on what precedes it, with signposting that makes the argumentative structure visible. This is required in long essays, dissertations and theses, where structures organised by topic or by source often fail to build an argument.
masteryEvidence: Produces a plan in which each section's sub-claim is stated and its contribution to the main position explained
Orders sub-claims by logical dependence (e.g. establishing a definition or fact before evaluating a policy)
Places counter-arguments where they are most relevant rather than in a single detached section
Uses section and paragraph openings to signal argumentative moves, not just topics
Revises a topic-based or source-by-source structure into an argument-based one
topics.assessmentPrompt: Ask the learner to reverse-outline a draft of 2,000 words or more by writing the claim (not the topic) of each section in one sentence. Check whether each claim contributes to the main position, whether the order reflects logical dependence, and whether any section is purely descriptive.

topics.name: Rhetorical appeals
topics.description: Recognise and use appeals to reason (logos), to the writer's credibility (ethos) and to the reader's values and emotions (pathos) as they operate in academic contexts, where logos dominates but credibility is built through accurate citation, calibrated claims and disciplinary language, and value appeals are usually restrained. Recognising appeals helps learners read persuasive texts critically and adjust persuasion for academic and public audiences.
masteryEvidence: Identifies logos, ethos and pathos appeals in a short persuasive text and explains their intended effect
Explains how academic writers construct credibility through citation, hedging, methodological transparency and disciplinary terminology
Distinguishes appropriate value appeals in academic writing (stating significance or ethical stakes) from emotive language that would undermine credibility
Adjusts the balance of appeals when adapting an academic argument for a non-specialist audience
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner two introductions to the same argument — one from an academic article, one from a campaigning website. Ask how each builds credibility and engages the reader, and which features would be inappropriate in the other context. Look for specific linguistic evidence (citations, hedges, emotive adjectives, direct address) rather than general impressions.

topics.name: Argument mapping
topics.description: Represent the structure of an argument as a diagram of claims, reasons, co-premises and objections, showing how each supports or challenges another, in order to analyse a source's reasoning or to plan one's own. Mapping externalises reasoning that is otherwise held in working memory, making gaps, unstated premises and weak links visible.
masteryEvidence: Produces a map of a short source argument that distinguishes the main claim, reasons, co-premises and objections
Identifies unstated premises while mapping and adds them explicitly
Distinguishes reasons that support a claim independently from those that work only jointly
Uses a map of their own planned argument to find unsupported sub-claims before drafting
Converts a map into a linear outline or paragraph sequence
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner a 150-word argumentative paragraph and ask for a box-and-arrow map. Check that the main claim is at the top, that reasons connect to the claims they support, that at least one implicit premise is made explicit, and that any objection is shown as opposing rather than supporting.

topics.name: Arguing orally
topics.description: Construct, support and defend arguments in real-time academic talk — seminars, tutorials, Q&A sessions and supervision — by stating positions concisely, supporting them with reasons and sources, responding to challenges, and conceding or refining positions as discussion develops. Oral argument differs from written argument in its pace, its co-construction across speakers and its reliance on mitigation to maintain collegiality.
masteryEvidence: States a position with at least one reason and supporting evidence within a single turn
Responds to a challenge by clarifying, defending with evidence or conceding part of the point, without withdrawing from the discussion
Builds on or disputes a previous speaker's point explicitly, with appropriate mitigation
Refers to readings or data orally to support a point
Revises a position in response to a stronger argument and signals the revision
topics.assessmentPrompt: In a small-group discussion, have a peer or the teacher challenge the learner's stated view with a counter-example. Observe whether the learner acknowledges the challenge, responds with a reason or evidence, and either maintains or explicitly refines the position, using mitigated language.

topics.name: Exploratory and adversarial argument
topics.description: Distinguish argument as collaborative, open-ended inquiry — exploring a question, testing ideas and reaching provisional conclusions — from argument as persuasive advocacy for a settled position, and recognise which orientation a genre, task or interaction calls for. Many academic genres and events (discussion essays, literature reviews, seminars) are largely exploratory, whereas others (debates, proposals, policy briefs) are more adversarial.
masteryEvidence: Classifies academic tasks and genres according to whether they primarily call for exploratory or adversarial argument
Explains how stance, hedging and treatment of alternatives differ between the two orientations
Adapts a persuasive paragraph into an exploratory one, and vice versa, by changing framing, hedging and treatment of alternatives
Contributes to a seminar in exploratory mode, offering tentative ideas and building on others' contributions
topics.assessmentPrompt: Show the learner two short texts on the same question — a debate speech and a literature review paragraph. Ask how their purposes and their treatment of opposing views differ. Look for recognition that the review weighs views to map a field and reach a provisional judgement, whereas the speech advocates and minimises opposition.

topics.name: Evaluating arguments
topics.description: Judge the quality of an argument by assessing whether its premises are acceptable, relevant to the conclusion and jointly sufficient to support it, whether its warrants hold, and how well it deals with objections — and express that judgement in measured academic language. This is the core analytical move in critical reviews, literature reviews and peer review.
masteryEvidence: Assesses a source's argument separately for acceptability of premises, relevance and sufficiency of support
Identifies the weakest link in an argument and explains its effect on the conclusion
Distinguishes a poorly argued case from a conclusion one disagrees with
Writes a balanced evaluative paragraph that acknowledges strengths and limitations with reasons
Applies scheme-specific critical questions, for example to arguments from expert opinion or analogy
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner a 250-word argumentative extract and ask for a 100-word evaluation identifying one strength and the single most serious weakness, with reasons. Look for evaluation based on relevance, sufficiency or acceptability of support rather than on agreement with the conclusion, and for measured evaluative language.

topics.name: Critical thinking in academic contexts
topics.description: Understand critical thinking in university study as a contested cluster of practices and dispositions — questioning claims, weighing evidence, judging reasoning and acknowledging uncertainty — whose concrete form varies by discipline and task. Treating it as explicit, learnable academic practice rather than a personal or cultural trait lets learners see what markers actually reward.
masteryEvidence: Explains, with an example from their own field, what a tutor is likely to mean by 'be more critical' in a specific piece of feedback
Distinguishes critical engagement (questioning, weighing, qualifying, acknowledging strengths) from fault-finding or unsupported personal opinion
Identifies at least two ways in which expectations of criticality differ between two disciplines or two assessment types
Describes critical thinking as a set of practices that can be learned and made explicit, not a fixed trait of individuals or groups
topics.assessmentPrompt: Show the learner two short student paragraphs on the same source — one summarising it accurately, one summarising it and then questioning the generalisability of its sample — together with the tutor comment 'needs more critical engagement'. Ask which paragraph responds to the comment and why. Look for reference to questioning evidence, scope or reasoning rather than to tone, length or 'adding my opinion'.

topics.name: Description, analysis and evaluation
topics.description: Distinguish three kinds of academic move — describing what something is or says, analysing how or why it works (its parts, causes, relationships and implications) and evaluating its value, validity or significance against stated criteria — and recognise which moves a task and its markers expect. Most 'too descriptive' feedback signals an imbalance among these moves rather than a lack of knowledge.
masteryEvidence: Labels sentences in a student paragraph as descriptive, analytical or evaluative and justifies each label
Rewrites a descriptive sentence about a source or dataset as an analytical sentence (explaining a cause, mechanism or relationship) and as an evaluative sentence (judging against a named criterion)
Identifies which moves an assignment brief's command words require and roughly in what proportion
Explains why some description remains necessary as the basis for analysis and evaluation, and keeps it subordinate to them in their own writing
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner a 120-word paragraph from a student essay that is mostly summary. Ask them to mark each sentence D, A or E and then add two sentences: one analytical and one evaluative. Check that the analytical sentence explains how or why rather than adding detail, and that the evaluative sentence names a criterion (e.g. sample size, relevance, consistency with other findings) rather than offering unsupported opinion.

topics.name: Critical questioning
topics.description: Habitually interrogate claims, texts, data and one's own ideas with questions such as how do we know, according to whom, compared with what, under what conditions and so what. Questioning is the generative engine of critical reading, analysis and research, and can be practised as a deliberate routine before it becomes a disposition.
masteryEvidence: Generates, unprompted, questions about the evidence, source, scope and implications of a short text or claim, going beyond comprehension questions
Selects the two or three questions most consequential for a given task rather than applying a full checklist mechanically
Formulates questions accurately and with enough mitigation to use them in seminars, supervision and peer review
Applies the same questions to their own draft claims, not only to other people's texts
Turns a productive question into a line of inquiry, such as a targeted search, a comparison or a paragraph
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner a one-sentence, headline-style claim containing a statistic and two minutes to write as many questions about it as they can. Then ask them to star the one question whose answer would most change their judgement. Look for questions about source, sample, comparison, causation and scope, and for a starred choice the learner can justify.

topics.name: Types and strength of evidence
topics.description: Recognise the main kinds of evidence used in academic argument — experimental and statistical data, qualitative accounts, documentary and textual evidence, expert testimony and anecdote — and judge what each can and cannot establish for a particular claim. Evidence hierarchies, such as those used in evidence-based medicine, are useful but field-bound tools, not universal rankings.
masteryEvidence: Classifies the evidence offered in a short text by type and states what kind of claim each type can support
Explains why a single case, anecdote or quotation cannot by itself support a general claim, while recognising its value for illustration or hypothesis generation
Describes an evidence hierarchy used in a particular field and at least one limitation of applying it elsewhere
Distinguishes the strength of a piece of evidence from the authority or prestige of its source
Replaces weaker evidence with stronger, claim-appropriate evidence when revising their own writing
topics.assessmentPrompt: Present four pieces of evidence for one claim: a personal anecdote, an expert quoted in a newspaper, a survey of 2,000 people and a randomised trial. Ask the learner to rank them for a claim about a treatment's effect, then for a claim about how participants experienced the treatment. Check that the ranking changes with the claim, showing that evidential strength is relative to what is being argued.

topics.name: Deductive, inductive and abductive reasoning
topics.description: Recognise and use the main patterns of inference: deduction, in which the conclusion follows necessarily if the premises are true; induction, which generalises or predicts from observed cases with probability rather than certainty; and abduction, which infers the most plausible explanation for observations. Knowing which pattern an argument uses tells the reader what degree of certainty it can claim and how it might fail.
masteryEvidence: Identifies whether a short argument is deductive, inductive or abductive and justifies the identification
Explains why a valid deductive argument can still reach a false conclusion if a premise is false
Judges an inductive generalisation by the size and representativeness of the cases and by the existence of counter-cases
Proposes at least one rival explanation when evaluating an inference to the best explanation
Calibrates the certainty of their own conclusions to the type of inference used, through modal verbs, reporting verbs and hedges
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give three short arguments: a syllogism with a doubtful premise, a generalisation from a small convenience survey and an explanation of an unexpected result. Ask the learner to name each type, state the main way each could fail and rewrite each conclusion with appropriate certainty. Look for recognition that only deduction can guarantee its conclusion and that the others need hedged conclusions.

topics.name: Correlation and causation
topics.description: Distinguish associations between variables from causal relationships by considering confounding, reverse causation, chance and selection effects, and know in broad terms which research designs (randomised experiments, natural experiments, controlled longitudinal designs) can support causal claims. This underpins accurate reading and reporting of research and the choice of causal verbs in writing.
masteryEvidence: Explains, by naming a plausible confounding variable, why a reported correlation may not reflect a causal effect
Identifies reverse causation or selection as alternative explanations for a given association
States what kind of design would be needed to support a causal claim in a given scenario
Rewrites an overclaimed causal sentence into one matched to the evidence (e.g. 'is associated with', 'may contribute to')
Compares the causal language of a press report with the claims made in the original study
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner a news-style report: 'Students who sit at the front of lectures get higher marks.' Ask for two alternative explanations and an accurately hedged rewrite of the headline. Look for a confounder (e.g. prior motivation), reverse causation or self-selection, and wording such as 'is associated with' rather than 'leads to'.

topics.name: Recognising fallacies
topics.description: Recognise common informal fallacies — straw man, ad hominem, false dilemma, hasty generalisation, slippery slope, appeal to popularity and post hoc reasoning — as misuses of otherwise legitimate argument patterns, and explain what makes a particular instance fallacious in its context. The aim is diagnostic precision when evaluating and constructing arguments, not label-spotting.
masteryEvidence: Identifies a fallacy in a short argument and explains in their own words why the reasoning fails in that context
Distinguishes a legitimate use of a pattern (a relevant appeal to expert opinion, a justified challenge to a source's credibility) from a fallacious one
Repairs a fallacious argument by supplying missing evidence, omitted alternatives or appropriate qualification
Detects straw-man representations of sources in their own and peers' drafts
topics.assessmentPrompt: Provide two short arguments that both question a researcher's credibility: one because of an undisclosed financial interest directly related to the finding, the other because of the researcher's nationality. Ask which is fallacious and why. Look for an explanation based on relevance to the claim, rather than the label 'ad hominem' applied to both.

topics.name: Cognitive biases
topics.description: Understand how systematic tendencies in human judgement — especially confirmation bias and motivated reasoning, but also availability and anchoring — shape what we search for, notice, believe and report, and adopt procedural safeguards in reading and research, such as seeking disconfirming evidence, setting criteria in advance and inviting others' scrutiny. Awareness alone rarely removes bias; routines help.
masteryEvidence: Describes confirmation bias and one other bias with an example drawn from academic reading or research
Identifies where their own literature search or source selection may have been skewed towards confirming sources
Applies at least one safeguard, such as a deliberate search for counter-evidence or pre-defined inclusion criteria
Distinguishes cognitive bias in reasoning from bias as a source's interests or perspective
topics.assessmentPrompt: Ask the learner how they found the sources for their latest assignment, then ask: 'What search would you run to find evidence against your thesis?' Look for a concrete counter-search (terms, databases, filters) and recognition that the original search terms may have presupposed the conclusion.

topics.name: Considering multiple perspectives
topics.description: Identify the range of defensible positions on an issue and represent each fairly — including those one rejects — in terms its proponents would recognise, before weighing them against explicit criteria. Fair representation is a precondition for credible counter-argument, synthesis and discussion writing, and protects against straw-man reasoning.
masteryEvidence: Identifies at least three distinct positions on a debated issue and the main reason or value behind each
Summarises an opposing view accurately enough that a proponent would accept the summary
Attributes perspectives clearly with reporting language, keeping them distinct from the writer's own view
Explains how differences in values, interests, disciplines or contexts give rise to different positions
Weighs perspectives against explicit criteria rather than simply listing them
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner a contested issue from their field and ask for a two-sentence summary of the strongest version of the view they disagree with. Check accuracy and charity (would a proponent accept it?), clear attribution and the absence of loaded or dismissive wording.

topics.name: Beliefs about knowledge
topics.description: Reflect on and develop one's beliefs about the nature of knowledge — its certainty, simplicity, source and justification — moving from treating knowledge as fixed facts transmitted by authorities, through treating all views as equally valid, towards evaluating claims as better or worse supported. These beliefs shape how learners read conflicting sources, respond to open questions and feedback, and build arguments.
masteryEvidence: Explains, with an example, why two credible sources might reach different conclusions
Distinguishes 'all opinions are equally valid' from 'claims can be compared by the quality of their support'
Responds to conflicting sources by comparing evidence and reasoning, rather than by choosing the more authoritative source or declaring the issue a matter of opinion
Describes how what counts as knowledge differs between at least two disciplines
Uses provisional language appropriately where knowledge in a field is contested
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give two short abstracts that reach conflicting conclusions on the same question and ask: 'Which should we believe, and how would you decide?' Note whether the learner defers to authority or recency (absolutist), treats the matter as opinion (multiplist) or proposes criteria such as design, sample and context (evaluativist).

topics.name: Evaluating theories and models
topics.description: Evaluate a theory, model or framework against criteria such as explanatory power, scope, empirical support, internal coherence, parsimony and usefulness for a stated purpose, and compare rival frameworks on those criteria. This moves learners from reporting what a theory says to justifying why they use, adapt or reject it.
masteryEvidence: Applies at least three named criteria to evaluate a theory or model used in their field
Distinguishes the evidence for a theory from the theory itself and identifies evidence that would challenge it
Compares two rival frameworks on explicit criteria and reaches a qualified judgement for a stated purpose
Identifies the scope conditions under which a model applies and where its assumptions break down
Justifies the choice of a theoretical framework for their own project against at least one alternative
topics.assessmentPrompt: Ask the learner to name a model widely used in their field and give one strength and one limitation, each tied to a criterion and to evidence or a case. Look for criterion-based judgement and awareness of scope, rather than 'it is old' or 'it is too simple'.

topics.name: Applying theory to cases
topics.description: Use concepts, theories or models as analytical tools to explain a case, dataset, text or situation: selecting a relevant concept, mapping its components onto specific evidence, and drawing out what the analysis reveals, including where the case does not fit. Application is the core move in case studies, problem questions and many dissertation analyses.
masteryEvidence: Selects a concept or model appropriate to the question and justifies the choice
Maps each component of the model onto specific features of the case, citing case evidence for each
Moves between abstract concept and concrete detail within paragraphs rather than presenting theory and case in separate blocks
Identifies at least one aspect of the case that the model explains poorly and comments on its implications
Draws a conclusion or recommendation that follows from the analysis rather than from general knowledge
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give a 200-word case and a simple model with three or four components, and ask for one analytical paragraph. Check whether each component is linked to specific case evidence, whether the paragraph moves between concept and case, and whether any limitation of fit is noted, rather than the model being described and the case then retold.

topics.name: Analytical problem-solving
topics.description: Define a problem precisely (its symptoms, causes, stakeholders and constraints), generate a range of possible responses, evaluate them against explicit criteria such as effectiveness, feasibility, cost and ethics, and justify a recommendation with its trade-offs acknowledged. This process underlies problem–solution essays, case analyses, design reports and policy writing.
masteryEvidence: Distinguishes a problem's symptoms from its causes in a written problem statement
Generates more than one plausible response before evaluating any of them
Evaluates options against explicit, defined criteria and records trade-offs
Justifies a recommendation with reference to the criteria and acknowledges its risks or limitations
Organises a written or spoken analysis using a situation–problem–response–evaluation structure
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give a short scenario (e.g. low uptake of a university writing centre). Ask the learner for a two-sentence problem definition and three options, each with one criterion-based reason for and against. Look for a cause-focused definition, genuinely different options and explicit criteria, rather than an immediate single solution.

topics.name: Reflexivity and positionality
topics.description: Recognise how one's own position — background, experiences, values, languages, disciplinary training and relationship to participants — shapes the questions asked, the evidence noticed and the interpretations made, and account for this transparently. Reflexivity is expected in qualitative and practice-based research and increasingly in reflective and critical genres across disciplines.
masteryEvidence: Identifies specific aspects of their own position that could influence a particular research or interpretive decision
Explains how a differently positioned researcher might interpret the same data differently, and why
Distinguishes reflexive accounting for one's position from autobiographical narrative and from claims of bias-free objectivity
Describes concrete practices (e.g. reflexive memos, peer debriefing, participant checking) used to examine their influence
Judges how much reflexive commentary a given genre and discipline expect
topics.assessmentPrompt: Ask the learner to write three sentences on how their own background might shape their interpretation of interviews in a planned project. Look for specific, research-relevant features (e.g. shared language with participants, insider status) linked to particular effects and a mitigating practice, rather than a general admission of 'bias' or a life story.

topics.name: Academic and writer identity
topics.description: Understand that academic writing and speaking construct an identity — through choices of stance, self-mention, citation, register and topic — and that entering a discipline involves negotiating new identities alongside existing ones. Seeing identity as discoursally constructed helps learners make deliberate choices about how they present themselves, and makes tensions between existing selves and academic conventions discussable rather than private.
masteryEvidence: Identifies linguistic choices in a text that construct the writer as, for example, a cautious researcher, an authoritative expert or a student reporting others' work
Describes how they want to present themselves in a specific assignment and the linguistic choices that would achieve this
Explains the distinction between autobiographical self, discoursal self and self as author with examples from their own writing
Articulates tensions between existing identities and disciplinary expectations and identifies options for negotiating them
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner two short paragraphs reporting the same finding — one using 'I argue', calibrated hedges and evaluative citation, the other using impersonal constructions and heavy reliance on sources. Ask what kind of writer each constructs, which they would choose for a named assignment, and why. Look for links between specific linguistic features and identity effects, and a choice justified by genre and discipline.

topics.name: Drawing on a plurilingual repertoire
topics.description: Use all one's languages strategically for academic learning — reading and note-making across languages, discussing ideas in shared languages, planning with the first language and checking terminology bilingually — while producing assessed work in the required language and within institutional rules. Treating the repertoire as an integrated resource supports comprehension, conceptual depth and confidence.
masteryEvidence: Describes how they currently use each of their languages in study and evaluates which uses help or hinder learning
Uses sources in other languages to build conceptual understanding alongside English sources, checking key terms across languages
Plans or brainstorms in any language and transforms the plan into well-formed English academic text
Uses shared languages productively in group work while keeping peers who do not share them included
Distinguishes permitted plurilingual strategies from uses that breach module rules, such as submitting machine-translated text where this is prohibited
topics.assessmentPrompt: Ask the learner to describe the process behind a recent piece of writing: which languages they used, at which stages and for what. Look for purposeful, stage-specific uses (e.g. first-language reading for background, bilingual term checks, English drafting), awareness of risks and rules, and an explanation of why each use helped.

topics.name: English as a lingua franca in academia
topics.description: Understand that much academic communication in English takes place among multilingual users for whom English is a shared additional language; that effectiveness in such interaction depends on intelligibility, accommodation and negotiation of meaning rather than conformity to a native-speaker model; and that all participants, including first-language English users, share responsibility for mutual understanding.
masteryEvidence: Explains the difference between communicative effectiveness in lingua franca interaction and conformity to native-speaker norms, with examples
Uses accommodation strategies (rephrasing, adjusting pace, avoiding local idioms, checking understanding) with interlocutors from varied language backgrounds
Distinguishes non-standard forms that impede understanding from those that do not
Identifies contexts, such as assessed writing and publication, where institutional norms still apply, and explains the tension
topics.assessmentPrompt: Show a short transcript in which one student's idiom causes a breakdown and another student's non-standard grammatical form causes none. Ask which feature mattered for communication and how the breakdown could have been avoided. Look for an intelligibility-based explanation and a concrete accommodation strategy.

topics.name: Intercultural communication
topics.description: Manage differences in expectations, communication styles and assumptions in academic interaction with peers, tutors and supervisors by noticing when misunderstanding may stem from differing norms, suspending quick judgements, checking interpretations and negotiating shared ways of working. Intercultural competence here treats culture as dynamic and multiple — institutional, disciplinary and group-level as well as national — rather than as fixed national traits.
masteryEvidence: Offers more than one interpretation of a misunderstanding in academic interaction, including institutional, disciplinary and individual explanations
Uses clarification and talk about the interaction itself to negotiate expectations (e.g. agreeing how a group will divide work and communicate)
Avoids attributing individuals' behaviour to national stereotypes when discussing group or seminar dynamics
Adapts communication style to a new context while retaining choices about their own norms
Recognises that departments, programmes and project groups develop their own norms that all newcomers must learn
topics.assessmentPrompt: Present a short scenario, such as a group member who does not reply in the project chat or a student who is silent in seminars. Ask the learner for three possible explanations and what they would do. Look for explanations beyond national culture, a non-judgemental checking strategy and a proportionate action.

topics.name: Intercultural rhetoric
topics.description: Understand how views of rhetorical variation across languages and cultures have developed — from Kaplan's contrastive rhetoric, through Connor's intercultural rhetoric, to critical contrastive rhetoric — and use this to analyse why writing conventions differ and change, without assuming that any culture's rhetoric is deficient or that an individual's writing is determined by their first language. The practical outcome is treating conventions as learnable, situated choices.
masteryEvidence: Summarises Kaplan's 1966 claims and at least two major critiques of them (e.g. essentialism, reliance on L2 student essays, privileging of English norms)
Explains how intercultural rhetoric shifts attention from national cultures to genres, disciplines, small cultures and the interaction around texts
Compares the organisation of texts in one genre across two languages or contexts, attributing differences to genre, purpose, audience and schooling rather than to fixed thought patterns
Identifies which English-medium academic writing expectations in their discipline differ from conventions they have learnt elsewhere and treats them as conventions rather than universal standards
topics.assessmentPrompt: Ask the learner to describe a difference they have noticed between academic writing in another language or context and English-medium study, and then what other explanations (genre, discipline, schooling, audience, individual style) might account for it. Look for movement away from claims that 'people from X think in a particular way' towards situated, multi-factor explanations.

topics.name: Linguistic diversity as resource
topics.description: Recognise and challenge deficit framings that treat multilingual students as lacking (language, critical thinking, autonomy), and understand linguistic and cultural diversity as a resource for learning, collaboration and knowledge-making. For learners, this means recognising the assets in their own repertoires and experience; for programmes, it means making academic expectations explicit for all students rather than remediating some.
masteryEvidence: Identifies deficit framings in descriptions of international or multilingual students (e.g. in group-work comments or media reports) and explains why they are problematic
Describes specific resources their own linguistic and educational background brings to their study
Explains why academic literacy conventions are new to most students, including first-language English users
Contributes perspectives or sources from other linguistic contexts to discussions and assignments where relevant
topics.assessmentPrompt: Show a statement such as 'International students struggle with critical thinking and need remedial support.' Ask the learner to evaluate it. Look for identification of the overgeneralisation, recognition that criticality is a learnable academic convention that is new to many students, and an alternative framing based on explicit teaching for all.

topics.name: Standards, native-speakerism and legitimacy
topics.description: Examine critically the assumption that native-speaker English is the benchmark for academic English, distinguishing the conventions of academic genres (which all writers must learn) from nativeness, and understanding how native-speakerism, gatekeeping and language ideologies affect assessment, publication and participation. This enables learners to claim legitimacy as multilingual academic users while making informed choices about conventions.
masteryEvidence: Distinguishes features expected because of genre and disciplinary convention from those expected merely because they sound native-like
Explains native-speakerism and gives an example of how it can operate in academic settings (feedback, peer assessment, group roles)
Evaluates institutional language policies or feedback comments for assumptions about native-speaker norms
Describes how multilingual scholars navigate English-medium publishing, including the role of literacy brokers and the inequities involved
Makes and justifies informed choices about when to conform to and when to question conventions in their own writing
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner two tutor comments on a draft sentence: 'Awkward — not how a native speaker would say it' and 'Unclear: who carried out this process?' Ask which is more useful feedback and why. Look for recognition that the second targets communicative clarity, whereas the first invokes nativeness without identifying the problem.

dependencies.reason: Recognising an argument depends on distinguishing claims from facts, opinions and evidence
Classifying claims presupposes understanding what a claim is within an argument
Claims of definition draw on the rhetorical function of defining and its formal patterns
Causal claims are recognised and formulated through the language of cause and effect
Toulmin's layout analyses the internal structure of arguments, which requires the basic concept of argument first
Supporting claims operationalises the idea that an argument is a position backed by evidence and reasoning
Choosing appropriate support depends on knowing what different kinds of evidence can establish
Examples are a common form of support whose language and representativeness learners need to control
The notion of a warrant as the link between data and claim comes from the Toulmin model
Learners must be able to attach evidence to claims before they can articulate the reasoning that connects them
Warrants are typically expressed through the language of reasons and mechanisms
Objections target a claim's support, so learners must first have built supported claims
Generating strong objections depends on identifying and fairly representing positions other than one's own
One can only concede or rebut objections that have first been identified
Concession–rebuttal sequences are realised through concessive and adversative language
Understanding how writers contract and expand dialogic space explains how concession can coexist with a firm stance
A defensible position is one that can be supported; learners must be able to support individual claims first
Positions are taken in relation to the range of views on a question, which learners need to survey first
Stating a position at the right strength depends on calibrating claims to evidence
An extended argument is organised around a sustained main position
Placing responses to objections within a long text requires control of the concession and rebuttal moves themselves
Claim–counterclaim and problem–solution patterns provide text-level structures for sequencing an argument
Mapping sub-claims and their dependencies is a practical way to plan the sequence of a long argument
Appeals are understood as means of persuasion within an argument
In academic writing, credibility and reader engagement are realised largely through metadiscourse resources
Mapping a source requires first locating its claims, reasons, evidence and conclusions
Learners map support relations more accurately once they understand how claims and support connect
Arguing orally builds on the ability to state and justify a view in discussion
Responding to challenges collegially requires mitigated agreement and disagreement
Real-time defence of a position transfers concession and rebuttal moves usually first practised in writing
Contrasting two orientations of argument presupposes the general concept of argument
Exploratory argument consists largely in representing and weighing several perspectives
Valuing provisional, inquiry-oriented argument depends on seeing knowledge as constructed and open to revision
Judging whether support is relevant and sufficient requires identifying the reasoning that links it to the claim
Recognising common fallacies supplies ready diagnoses of why some support fails
Evaluating an argument includes judging the relevance, sufficiency and quality of the evidence it offers
Mapping an argument before evaluating it separates its structure from agreement with its conclusion
Criticality is introduced as one of the general expectations of university learners before it is unpacked as a contested set of practices
The three-way distinction operationalises the general notion of criticality into recognisable textual moves
Recognising which moves a task requires depends on knowing what command words such as 'analyse', 'evaluate' and 'outline' demand
Analytical sentences are largely realised through the language of reasons, mechanisms and rationales
Critical questions are the means of moving from description to analysis and evaluation, so learners need the target moves in view
Questioning a text's claims requires first identifying which statements are its central claims
Judging types and strength of evidence presupposes distinguishing evidence from claims and opinions in a text
Knowing empirical, review, theoretical and popular source types helps learners see what kind of evidence a source can provide
Classifying inference patterns requires the prior concept of an argument as premises or reasons leading to a conclusion
Deductive and hypothetical reasoning is typically expressed through conditional structures that learners must parse and produce
Distinguishing association from causation depends on control of causal language and of the strength of causal claims
Learners need the meaning of correlation, sample and significance before reasoning about what correlational findings show
Judging causal claims applies the general principle that evidential strength depends on how the evidence was produced
A fallacy is a defective argument, so learners must first understand what an argument is
Several fallacies (hasty generalisation, post hoc) are failures of inductive or causal inference and are best understood against those patterns
Biases such as confirmation bias distort how evidence is sought and weighed, which assumes a prior sense of what good evidence is
The main safeguards against bias are questioning routines turned on one's own reasoning
Representing a view fairly requires tracking whose view a text expresses and how strongly it is endorsed
Fair representation of a position depends on accurate condensation of what its proponents actually say
Asking 'according to whom?' and 'who would disagree?' is the routine that surfaces alternative perspectives
Beliefs about knowledge are introduced as one of the dispositional foundations of academic criticality
Moving beyond 'it's all opinion' requires criteria for comparing the support behind competing claims
Evaluating theories assumes an evaluativist view in which frameworks are constructed, provisional and comparable on reasoned criteria
Learners usually judge a theory's explanatory power and scope after having used it to analyse cases
Criteria such as explanatory power and testability draw on abductive and inductive reasoning about how theories relate to evidence
Applying a model to a case is an analytical move that learners must be able to distinguish from describing the model or retelling the case
A concept can only be mapped onto evidence once its definition and distinguishing features are clear
Learners typically meet the concepts they apply in dense theoretical readings that they must first understand
The situation–problem–response–evaluation language gives learners a frame for expressing each stage of the process
Defining a problem precisely depends on asking why it occurs, for whom and under what constraints
Evaluating options requires judging what evidence shows that a response is likely to work
Reflexivity presupposes that knowledge is constructed by positioned knowers rather than simply discovered
Recognising one's own view as one perspective builds on the practice of representing others' perspectives
Understanding systematic distortions in judgement helps learners see why examining their own influence on research is necessary
Learners usually meet concrete choices about impersonality and authorial presence before reflecting on how such choices construct identity
The academic literacies view of writing as social practice involving identity and power frames identity as a legitimate object of study
The academic literacies critique of deficit 'study skills' models provides the basis for resource-oriented views of student diversity
Deficit framings are most often encountered and internalised during transition to a new educational context, which learners need to have reflected on
Using all one's languages strategically depends on first seeing the multilingual repertoire as an asset rather than an interference
Plurilingual strategies are a subset of learning strategies that learners select and orchestrate deliberately
Understanding lingua franca effectiveness builds on rejecting deficit views of non-native varieties
The distinction between accent and intelligibility underpins the lingua franca focus on mutual understanding
Academic intercultural interaction typically takes place in English as a lingua franca, where accommodation is a shared responsibility
Checking interpretations, the core intercultural repair move, depends on confirmation and clarification resources
Intercultural rhetoric explains rhetorical variation largely through genre and discourse community, so the genre concept must come first
Comparing rhetorical conventions requires the ability to recognise how texts are organised
Seeing variation across disciplines within English helps learners avoid attributing all rhetorical difference to national culture
Questioning native-speaker norms draws on lingua franca research showing that effectiveness does not depend on nativeness
Testing prescriptive style rules against actual practice is a concrete precursor to questioning broader standard-language ideologies

guidance.summary: Wingate's study found that students' understanding of 'argument' was often limited and that tutors' feedback used the term without explaining it; she proposes teaching argument as three components: the writer's position, the coherent presentation of that position, and its development through analysis and evaluation of knowledge and sources. Andrews stresses that argument in higher education takes discipline-specific forms, and Hirvela argues that L2 writing instruction has given argumentation less attention than its centrality warrants. Start by making explicit that most assessed writing is argumentative even when the task word is 'discuss' or 'explain'.

activities.title: Argument or not?
learnerActions: Sort short texts (news report, encyclopaedia entry, opinion blog, academic paragraph) into those that do and do not contain an argument
Justify each decision by pointing to a position and its support, or their absence
Draft a working definition of academic argument and test it on a new text
activities.intendedInsight: An argument needs a contestable position with support; accurate information alone is not an argument.
activities.rationale: Wingate's three-component model gives learners a concrete basis for recognising argument.

activities.title: Translating 'argument' in feedback
learnerActions: Examine tutor comments that use the word 'argument' on sample essays
Decide whether each comment concerns the position, its presentation or its development
Rewrite each comment as a specific revision action
activities.intendedInsight: 'Argument' in feedback refers to identifiable features that can be revised.
activities.rationale: Wingate found that feedback on argument was often too general for students to act on, and Andrews notes that tutors' expectations of argument vary across disciplines.

difficulties.pattern: 'An argument is a fight — it would be rude to argue in an essay.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Avoidance of any stance; reluctance to disagree with sources.
difficulties.response: Contrast everyday and academic senses of 'argument'; show measured, hedged arguments in exemplars.

difficulties.pattern: 'If I include all the relevant information, I have answered the question.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Comprehensive, well-organised but descriptive essays, often shaped by knowledge-display exams.
difficulties.response: Use exemplars to show that the question demands a position; have learners state their answer before planning content.

difficulties.pattern: 'Argument is only for argumentative essays, not for reports or lab write-ups.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Discussion sections that restate results without interpretation.
difficulties.response: Show the argument in a discussion section or a case report: the interpretation is a claim supported by results.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to state the argument of their most recent essay in one sentence.
diagnostic.strongResponse: A specific, contestable position that answers the question.
diagnostic.partialResponse: A topic statement such as 'This essay discusses the advantages and disadvantages of…'.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Cannot answer, or restates the essay title.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation and pre-sessional courses should establish the concept early and return to it in every writing task. In undergraduate in-sessional settings, show what argument looks like in each discipline's genres. PGT and PGR learners usually understand the concept but need to see how it applies to dissertations and research articles.

guidance.summary: The classical stasis tradition, adapted for composition teaching by Fahnestock and Secor, sorts claims into fact, definition, cause, value and policy, each with typical lines of support. Walton's argumentation schemes offer a complementary view: argument from verbal classification supports definitional claims, causal schemes support causal claims, and practical reasoning supports policy claims, each with its own critical questions. Teach claim types as a planning tool tied to assignment questions rather than as classification for its own sake.

activities.title: From question to claim type
learnerActions: Analyse six real assignment questions and identify the claim type or types each demands
List the kinds of support each claim type will need
Compare analyses and resolve disagreements
activities.intendedInsight: The type of claim a question invites predicts the kind of evidence and reasoning the answer needs.
activities.rationale: Fahnestock and Secor's stasis-based categories link claim types to characteristic forms of support.

activities.title: Unpacking a policy claim
learnerActions: Take a policy claim and list the factual, causal and value claims it presupposes
Order those claims so that each depends only on earlier ones
Turn the ordered list into an essay plan
activities.intendedInsight: Policy claims rest on chains of other claims that must be established first.
activities.rationale: Walton's account of practical reasoning shows that arguments for action depend on goals, means and consequences, each open to critical questions.

difficulties.pattern: Supporting a value claim ('X is the best approach') with description alone.
difficulties.revealedBy: Evaluative theses followed by paragraphs of description with no criteria.
difficulties.response: Require explicit criteria for every value claim and evidence against each criterion.

difficulties.pattern: 'According to the Oxford Dictionary, X means…' used to settle a contested concept.
difficulties.revealedBy: Dictionary definitions opening essays on contested disciplinary concepts.
difficulties.response: Show competing scholarly definitions and treat choosing a definition as a claim that needs justification.

diagnostic.task: Give the claim 'Social media should be regulated in the same way as tobacco' and ask what other claims must be established first.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Identifies claims about harm (fact/cause), comparability with tobacco (definition/analogy), values and feasibility.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Identifies harm only.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Restates agreement or disagreement with the claim.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation learners can use simplified claim types when planning short essays. Pre-sessional learners apply them to analysing essay questions. Undergraduates meet discipline-specific claim types (e.g. interpretive claims in the humanities); PGT learners in management, policy and health need policy and value claims in particular.
reviewNotes: The five-type taxonomy is a teaching heuristic from rhetoric and composition; real academic claims often combine types.

guidance.summary: Toulmin proposed his layout as a field-dependent alternative to formal logic, describing how practical arguments move from data to claim through warrants that may themselves need backing and that are limited by qualifiers and rebuttal conditions. Qin and Karabacak's analysis of Chinese EFL university students' argumentative essays used a modified Toulmin scheme and found that counter-argument and rebuttal elements were relatively infrequent but associated with higher-rated essays. Andrews cautions that the model analyses individual arguments rather than whole texts, so use it diagnostically and keep the terminology light at lower levels.

activities.title: Unpacking an argument
learnerActions: Label the elements of three short arguments taken from texts in their discipline
Reconstruct each implicit warrant in a sentence
Compare reconstructions across groups and discuss which warrants are contestable
activities.intendedInsight: Warrants are usually implicit and are often the point at which an argument can be challenged.
activities.rationale: Toulmin's model was designed to expose the warrant that licenses the move from data to claim.

activities.title: Finding the rebuttals
learnerActions: Code two student essays for claims, data, counter-arguments and rebuttals using a simplified scheme
Compare the higher-rated and lower-rated essays
Identify where a counter-argument and rebuttal could be added to the weaker essay
activities.intendedInsight: Higher-rated essays tend to acknowledge and respond to opposition rather than only stating claims and data.
activities.rationale: Qin and Karabacak found counter-argument and rebuttal elements associated with essay quality in their sample.

difficulties.pattern: Labelling the evidence itself as the warrant.
difficulties.revealedBy: Statistics or quotations identified as warrants in analysis tasks.
difficulties.response: Present the warrant as a general 'since…' or 'if…then…' principle connecting any such data to such a claim.

difficulties.pattern: 'My claim is… My data is… My warrant is…' — using the model as a paragraph template.
difficulties.revealedBy: Formulaic paragraphs that name the elements explicitly.
difficulties.response: Stress that the model is analytical; show how expert texts realise elements implicitly and in varied orders.

difficulties.pattern: Qualifiers limited to 'maybe' or 'I think'.
difficulties.revealedBy: A narrow hedging repertoire in analysis and writing.
difficulties.response: Teach a range of hedging devices and match them to the strength of data and warrant.

diagnostic.task: Give a short paragraph and ask the learner to identify its claim and the assumption that links its evidence to that claim.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Accurately states the implicit warrant and notes whether it is contestable.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Identifies claim and data but restates the data as the warrant.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Cannot identify the claim.

guidance.contextNotes: On pre-sessional courses, use a simplified version (claim, reason, evidence, objection, response). Undergraduates can use the full model to analyse readings and write critiques; PGT learners use it to examine research arguments, particularly in discussion sections.
reviewNotes: Evidence on the effect of explicit Toulmin instruction on L2 writing quality is mixed and context-specific; the model is presented as an analytical tool, not a proven intervention.

guidance.summary: Kuhn found that many people offered 'pseudoevidence' — plausible scenarios illustrating how something might happen — in place of evidence bearing on whether it is true; making this distinction explicit is central to teaching support. Wingate's account of argument places the development of a position through analysis of knowledge and sources at the centre of essay writing. At lower levels, paragraph scaffolds such as point–evidence–explanation can help, provided learners see that the explanation step does the argumentative work.

activities.title: Evidence or scenario?
learnerActions: Sort support items into research evidence, illustrative example and hypothetical scenario
Discuss what each can and cannot show
Rewrite a paragraph, replacing a scenario with evidence
activities.intendedInsight: A plausible story about how something could happen is not evidence that it does happen.
activities.rationale: Kuhn identified pseudoevidence as a common substitute for genuine evidence in everyday argument.

activities.title: Highlight the link
learnerActions: Highlight claim, evidence and explanation in their own paragraph in three colours
Identify any evidence that has no explanation next to it
Add or revise the explanation so that the link to the claim is explicit
activities.intendedInsight: Support requires an explicit link between evidence and claim.
activities.rationale: Wingate presents the development of a position through analysis of sources as a core component of argument.

difficulties.pattern: 'The quotation speaks for itself.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Quotations dropped into paragraphs without comment.
difficulties.response: Require a comment sentence after every quotation explaining its relevance. Do not ban quotation; teach integration.

difficulties.pattern: 'In my country…' or 'Everyone knows…' used as the main support.
difficulties.revealedBy: Personal experience and general knowledge used where research evidence is expected, often carried over from test essays.
difficulties.response: Show where personal experience is acceptable (e.g. reflective genres) and where research evidence is expected; practise locating sources for claims first supported by experience.

difficulties.pattern: Piling up citations without showing how each relates to the claim.
difficulties.revealedBy: Strings of parenthetical citations after general statements.
difficulties.response: Ask learners to state what each source contributes; reduce citations to those that do distinct work.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to support the claim 'Online learning can widen access to higher education' in three sentences.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Names a specific type of evidence, explains how it supports the claim and adds a qualification.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Gives an example or general statement without explaining the link.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Restates the claim in different words.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation learners benefit from PEEL-type scaffolds. Pre-sessional learners practise source-based support. Undergraduates learn disciplinary evidence norms; PGT learners must handle research evidence at higher density; PGR learners support original claims with their own data.

guidance.summary: In Toulmin's terms, warrants license the step from data to claim and may themselves require backing; writers often omit them because they seem obvious from their own perspective. Walton's argumentation schemes, each paired with critical questions, give learners a repertoire of common warrant types (from expert opinion, from cause to effect, from analogy, from consequences) and a way to anticipate where readers will push back. The writing goal is not to state every warrant, but to state those a reader in the discipline would not supply unaided.

activities.title: Same evidence, different claims
learnerActions: Examine one dataset and two opposing claims based on it
Write the warrant each claim needs
Decide which warrant is more defensible and explain why
activities.intendedInsight: Evidence does not speak for itself; the warrant determines what it supports.
activities.rationale: Toulmin shows that the same data can support different claims depending on the warrant invoked.

activities.title: Schemes and critical questions
learnerActions: Identify the argumentation scheme in a source argument (e.g. analogy, expert opinion)
Apply the scheme's critical questions
Add a warrant and backing to a paragraph of their own that uses the same scheme
activities.intendedInsight: Knowing the scheme predicts the objections a reader will raise and so which warrants need stating.
activities.rationale: Walton pairs each scheme with critical questions that expose its typical points of weakness.

difficulties.pattern: Leaving the link between evidence and claim implicit because it seems obvious to the writer.
difficulties.revealedBy: 'So what?' or 'How does this support your point?' comments; claims and evidence placed side by side.
difficulties.response: Ask a peer reader to mark every point where they cannot follow the reasoning; revise by adding warrants there.

difficulties.pattern: Explaining reasoning that expert readers already share.
difficulties.revealedBy: Over-explained, patronising passages after instruction on warrants, wasting word count.
difficulties.response: Calibrate with disciplinary exemplars: which links do expert writers leave implicit for their readers?

diagnostic.task: Give a paragraph with one missing warrant and ask the learner to find where a reader would ask 'Why does that follow?'
diagnostic.strongResponse: Locates the gap and supplies a plausible warrant, with backing if contestable.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Locates the gap but cannot articulate the warrant.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Sees no gap.

guidance.contextNotes: Pre-sessional learners can begin with simple 'this shows that… because…' frames. Undergraduates learn discipline-specific warrants. PGT learners writing for expert readers need to judge which warrants to state; PGR learners must defend conceptual and methodological warrants to examiners and reviewers.

guidance.summary: Kuhn's interviews showed that generating counter-arguments and alternative theories was among the weakest argument skills across age groups, which suggests it requires explicit teaching. Qin and Karabacak found counter-argument and rebuttal elements uncommon in their sample of EFL university essays but associated with higher quality, supporting deliberate attention. Effective practice separates generating strong objections — often by searching sources — from responding to them, which is taught next.

activities.title: Devil's advocate pairs
learnerActions: State a thesis to a partner
Listen while the partner raises the strongest objections they can
Record the objections, then swap roles
activities.intendedInsight: Others can see objections that writers miss in their own arguments.
activities.rationale: Kuhn's findings suggest that people seldom generate counter-arguments to their own views unprompted.

activities.title: Counter-source search
learnerActions: Search specifically for published sources that disagree with their thesis
Summarise the strongest counter-position fairly
Decide whether it must be addressed in the essay and where
activities.intendedInsight: Published counter-positions exist and readers will expect them to be engaged.
activities.rationale: Qin and Karabacak's results link the presence of counter-argument elements to higher-rated essays.

difficulties.pattern: 'Including counter-arguments will weaken my essay.'
difficulties.revealedBy: One-sided essays with no acknowledgement of other views.
difficulties.response: Show that addressing objections strengthens credibility, using higher-graded exemplars.

difficulties.pattern: 'Some people may say it is expensive, but this is not true.' — token objections.
difficulties.revealedBy: Weak, unsourced objections dismissed in a sentence.
difficulties.response: Require at least one sourced objection and ask peers to rate how damaging it is.

difficulties.pattern: A fixed 'Some people believe… However, I believe…' paragraph before the conclusion.
difficulties.revealedBy: Formulaic counter-argument paragraphs learned from test-preparation templates.
difficulties.response: Show how expert writers raise objections at the point where they are most relevant.

diagnostic.task: Give a thesis and ask for the strongest objection to it.
diagnostic.strongResponse: A substantive objection grounded in evidence or reasoning.
diagnostic.partialResponse: A plausible but weak or vague objection.
