diagnostic.strongResponse: Names a specific identity (e.g. a critical evaluator of policy) and concrete linguistic features that construct it.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Gives a vague aim ('professional', 'academic') with few linked features.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Shows no awareness that writing constructs an identity.

guidance.contextNotes: Pre-sessional courses can introduce identity through self-mention and stance choices. Undergraduates develop disciplinary voice; PGT learners often negotiate professional identities alongside academic ones; PGR learners build researcher identity and a scholarly voice, often across languages.

guidance.summary: García and Li Wei's account of translanguaging treats bilinguals' languages as an integrated repertoire and argues for pedagogies that leverage it rather than enforce strict separation; Canagarajah's translingual practice similarly emphasises the negotiation strategies through which multilingual users make meaning. The CEFR Companion Volume's plurilingual and pluricultural scales give institutional recognition to such competence. In EAP, the task is to help learners make these practices deliberate and transparent while meeting assessment requirements that usually require English output.

activities.title: Language-use audit
learnerActions: Map which languages they use at each stage of a study task (reading, note-making, discussing, planning, drafting)
Evaluate which uses help and which hinder
Share effective strategies with peers and choose one to try
activities.intendedInsight: Plurilingual practices are more effective when they are deliberate choices for specific purposes.
activities.rationale: García and Li Wei argue that learners' full repertoires can be mobilised for learning rather than suppressed.

activities.title: Bilingual concept glossary
learnerActions: Build a glossary of key disciplinary concepts with equivalents in their other languages
Note where meanings or connotations diverge
Discuss how these divergences affect understanding and translation
activities.intendedInsight: Cross-linguistic comparison deepens conceptual understanding and exposes false equivalents.
activities.rationale: The CEFR Companion Volume's plurilingual comprehension scale and Canagarajah's translingual practice both frame cross-language comparison as a competence.

difficulties.pattern: 'Using my first language is cheating and will slow down my English.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Guilt about first-language use; avoiding useful first-language resources, often after English-only classroom policies.
difficulties.response: Discuss the rationale for strategic first-language use and distinguish supportive strategies from wholesale translation of assessed work.

difficulties.pattern: Composing whole texts in the first language and then translating them.
difficulties.revealedBy: Calqued syntax, register mismatches and, where machine translation is used, possible breaches of module rules.
difficulties.response: Encourage first-language planning and note-making with English drafting; check module rules on translation tools. Do not ban first-language use outright.

difficulties.pattern: Group discussion slipping into a language some members do not share.
difficulties.revealedBy: Excluded group members; complaints about group dynamics.
difficulties.response: Have groups agree explicit language-use norms, including when a shared language is used and how its outcomes are reported to all members.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to describe a time when using another language helped them understand an academic concept, and how they checked their understanding.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Describes a specific strategy and a checking step (e.g. comparing definitions across languages).
diagnostic.partialResponse: Gives a vague description without any checking.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Says they never use other languages, or that they translate everything.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation learners, often new to English-medium study, benefit from explicit permission to use their repertoires. Pre-sessional courses can establish rules and strategies early. Undergraduates and PGT learners apply them in reading-heavy modules and multilingual groups; PGR learners often work with multilingual literatures and data, where transparent translation becomes a methodological issue.
reviewNotes: Institutional policies on machine translation and generative AI vary widely; learners must check module-level rules.

guidance.summary: Jenkins's research on the international university shows that, although students and staff communicate in English as a lingua franca, institutional language policies continue to assume native English norms. Mauranen's analysis of spoken academic English as a lingua franca documents how multilingual academics achieve understanding through explicitness, rephrasing and co-operative strategies. For EAP, this means teaching accommodation and negotiation strategies to all students — including first-language English users — while being honest about where normative expectations still apply in assessment.

activities.title: Breakdown or not?
learnerActions: Analyse transcripts of lingua franca academic exchanges
Identify features that did and did not cause breakdowns
Note the repair strategies speakers used
activities.intendedInsight: Understanding depends on intelligibility and co-operation, not on native-like form.
activities.rationale: Mauranen's corpus work documents the co-operative strategies that make academic lingua franca communication effective.

activities.title: Accommodation practice
learnerActions: In mixed groups, take turns explaining a disciplinary concept
Observers record accommodation moves (rephrasing, checking, slowing down)
Debrief on which moves helped most
activities.intendedInsight: Accommodation is a skill that all participants can develop and share responsibility for.
activities.rationale: Jenkins argues that responsibility for intelligibility in international universities should not rest only on non-native speakers.

difficulties.pattern: 'If I don't sound like a native speaker, I'm not communicating properly.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Reluctance to speak; excessive focus on accent.
difficulties.response: Refocus on intelligibility and the features that actually affect understanding.

difficulties.pattern: 'Lingua franca research means grammar doesn't matter in my essays.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Dismissal of feedback on written accuracy after learning about lingua franca communication.
difficulties.response: Distinguish spoken interaction from assessed written genres and discuss the tension openly.

difficulties.pattern: First-language English peers using fast speech and local idioms and expecting others to adapt.
difficulties.revealedBy: Breakdowns in mixed groups; multilingual students withdrawing from discussion.
difficulties.response: Include all students, including first-language English users, in accommodation training.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner what makes communication successful in a multilingual seminar.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Mentions mutual intelligibility, accommodation and checking understanding as shared responsibilities.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Mentions 'speaking correctly' together with some strategies.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Mentions only native-like accent and grammar.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation and pre-sessional cohorts are often highly multilingual, which makes lingua franca strategies immediately relevant. Undergraduates need them for group work with home students; PGT cohorts are typically very international; PGR learners use them at international conferences and in research collaborations.
reviewNotes: How far lingua franca findings should change expectations for assessed academic writing remains contested among EAP practitioners.

guidance.summary: Holliday's 'small cultures' approach treats culture as something that emerges in groups such as classrooms, departments and project teams, offering an alternative to large-culture national stereotypes. Zhou and colleagues' review of models of international students' adaptation (stress and coping, culture learning, social identification) shows that adjustment has affective, behavioural and cognitive dimensions. Teaching should therefore develop observation, interpretation and negotiation skills applicable in any new group, and should involve home and international students alike.

activities.title: Describe, interpret, evaluate
learnerActions: Read a critical incident from academic life (e.g. a group-work misunderstanding)
Describe what happened without judgement
Generate several interpretations, including institutional and individual ones, before evaluating
activities.intendedInsight: Suspending judgement and considering several explanations prevents premature cultural attribution.
activities.rationale: Holliday's small-cultures perspective directs attention to group and institutional explanations rather than national stereotypes.

activities.title: Group charter
learnerActions: At the start of a group project, negotiate explicit norms for communication channels, deadlines, turn-taking and language use
Record them in a short charter
Review the charter at the midpoint
activities.intendedInsight: Making norms explicit prevents differences from being attributed to individuals' or groups' character.
activities.rationale: The culture-learning approach reviewed by Zhou and colleagues emphasises learning the specific social skills a new context requires.

difficulties.pattern: 'Students from that country never speak in seminars.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Stereotyped explanations of peers' behaviour.
difficulties.response: Introduce small cultures and individual, situational and institutional explanations; ask for evidence for any generalisation.

difficulties.pattern: Withdrawal and isolation in the early weeks of study.
difficulties.revealedBy: Reduced participation, absence and reports of loneliness.
difficulties.response: Normalise adjustment difficulties, build structured peer contact, and refer to support services where appropriate.

difficulties.pattern: Assuming one's own communication norms are neutral and others' are odd.
difficulties.revealedBy: Judgements of peers as rude, passive or aggressive without reflection on one's own expectations.
difficulties.response: Have learners describe their own norms as one set among several and analyse an incident from both sides.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner how they would respond to a group member who seems not to be contributing.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Checks with the person, considers several explanations and proposes negotiating roles or norms.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Considers only one explanation.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Relies on a stereotype or moves straight to blame or complaint.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation and pre-sessional learners are often managing adjustment and multilingual groups simultaneously. Undergraduates need these skills in mixed home–international groups; PGT learners in intensive, highly international cohorts; PGR learners in supervision relationships and international research teams.
reviewNotes: Large-scale national culture-dimension frameworks are widely used in intercultural training but are criticised for essentialism; this record deliberately does not rely on them.

guidance.summary: Kaplan's 1966 article, with its diagrams of 'cultural thought patterns', was historically influential in drawing attention to rhetorical differences in L2 writing but has been heavily criticised for its ethnocentric framing, its reliance on L2 student essays and its static view of culture. Connor's reformulation as intercultural rhetoric widened the focus to genres, discourse communities, small cultures and the interaction around texts, and Kubota and Lehner's critical contrastive rhetoric argues that comparisons must attend to power, discourse and the essentialising of 'other' rhetorics. Hinds's reader/writer responsibility typology can be a useful lens on reading expectations but should not be applied to whole languages or nations.

activities.title: Critiquing Kaplan
learnerActions: Examine Kaplan's diagrams and his original claims
Read short summaries of the main critiques
Propose a better explanation for a rhetorical difference they have experienced
activities.intendedInsight: Rhetorical differences can be real, but explaining them through fixed national thought patterns stereotypes writers.
activities.rationale: Kubota and Lehner's critique shows how contrastive rhetoric can essentialise cultures and privilege English norms.

activities.title: Same genre, two contexts
learnerActions: Compare an abstract or introduction from their field published in another language with one published in English
Analyse the moves in each
Explain differences in terms of genre, audience, publication context and disciplinary norms
activities.intendedInsight: Genre, audience and context account for much rhetorical variation.
activities.rationale: Connor's intercultural rhetoric locates rhetorical variation in genres and contexts as well as in languages.

difficulties.pattern: 'My writing goes round in circles because I am from X.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Learners describing themselves through internalised versions of Kaplan-type stereotypes.
difficulties.response: Challenge the attribution; present conventions as learnable and relate differences to genre and schooling.

difficulties.pattern: 'English academic writing is simply logical; other traditions are illogical.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Hierarchical comparisons of writing traditions, by learners or in materials.
difficulties.response: Present English academic conventions as conventions and show variation within English across disciplines.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner why academic texts might be organised differently in different languages.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Refers to genre, audience, publication context and schooling, and notes variation within languages.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Mixes situated explanations with national generalisations.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Explains differences by fixed national thought patterns.

guidance.contextNotes: On pre-sessional courses, keep the treatment brief and practical, focused on conventions as learnable. Undergraduates and PGT learners benefit from comparing genres across their languages. PGR learners who publish internationally or read multilingual literatures can engage with the debate in more depth.
reviewNotes: Evidence for systematic cross-linguistic rhetorical differences exists for some genres and features, but findings vary with genre and corpus design; single studies should not be generalised to whole languages.

guidance.summary: Wingate argues for inclusive academic literacy instruction for all students rather than remedial provision targeted at international or 'non-traditional' students, since academic conventions are new to everyone entering a discipline. Leki's study of multilingual undergraduates in group projects showed how they could be positioned by peers as less competent, and Holliday's analysis of native-speakerism shows how such framings attribute deficits — in autonomy or critical thinking — to 'non-native' learners. Teaching should help learners recognise and resist deficit positioning while still acquiring the conventions they need.

activities.title: Reframing statements
learnerActions: Read statements about multilingual students taken from media, policies or peer comments
Identify deficit assumptions in each
Rewrite them as resource-oriented statements that also name what needs to be taught explicitly
activities.intendedInsight: How diversity is framed shapes expectations and opportunities.
activities.rationale: Wingate's case for inclusive practice and Holliday's critique of native-speakerism both identify deficit framing as a barrier.

activities.title: Repertoire assets map
learnerActions: Map their linguistic, educational, disciplinary and intercultural resources
Identify how two of these could contribute to a current module task
Share one contribution in a group discussion
activities.intendedInsight: Linguistic and cultural backgrounds offer concrete resources for academic work.
activities.rationale: Leki's findings show how multilingual students' contributions can be overlooked, which explicit asset-mapping helps counter.

difficulties.pattern: 'My English is bad, so my ideas are not worth sharing.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Silence, self-deprecation and reluctance to contribute.
difficulties.response: Separate the quality of ideas from language accuracy; show that contributions are valued and give structured opportunities to contribute.

difficulties.pattern: 'If diversity is a resource, accuracy doesn't matter.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Dismissal of language development goals after resource-oriented discussion.
difficulties.response: Present both as true: the repertoire is valued and academic English development remains a goal.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner what their language background brings to their studies.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Names specific assets (e.g. access to literature in another language, comparative perspectives).
diagnostic.partialResponse: Gives a generic answer ('different perspectives').
diagnostic.gapResponse: Names only difficulties.

guidance.contextNotes: At foundation and pre-sessional stages, emphasise confidence and assets during transition. Undergraduate in-sessional work should include home students and address group positioning. PGT learners benefit from using comparative perspectives in assignments; PGR learners from drawing on multilingual literatures and contexts.

guidance.summary: Holliday defines native-speakerism as an ideology that positions 'native-speaker' teachers and norms as the source of correct English and of good teaching methodology, often accompanied by the othering of 'non-native' learners. Jenkins's study of international universities shows how English language policies and entry requirements continue to assume native English norms despite lingua franca realities, and Lillis and Curry's study of multilingual scholars shows how English-medium publishing, including reliance on literacy brokers, reproduces inequities. EAP practitioners face a genuine tension between equipping learners with valued conventions and questioning norms; this topic makes that tension explicit rather than resolving it by fiat.

activities.title: Convention or nativeness?
learnerActions: Sort a set of feedback comments or editing changes into those grounded in genre convention or clarity and those grounded only in native-likeness
Discuss borderline cases
Rewrite one nativeness-based comment so that it identifies a communicative problem, or decide that no change is needed
activities.intendedInsight: Some expectations are legitimate genre conventions; others reflect an ideology of nativeness.
activities.rationale: Jenkins shows that academic English policies often conflate nativeness with standards.

activities.title: Literacy brokers and networks
learnerActions: Read a summary of research on literacy brokers in academic publishing
Map their own current and potential support networks for writing and publication
Discuss the ethics and practicalities of using each kind of support
activities.intendedInsight: Publishing involves mediation for most scholars; seeking help is normal, and access to help is unequal.
activities.rationale: Lillis and Curry document the role of literacy brokers in multilingual scholars' publishing.

difficulties.pattern: 'I will never be a legitimate academic writer because I'm not a native speaker.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Low confidence; over-reliance on proofreaders; reluctance to publish or present.
difficulties.response: Locate legitimacy in disciplinary expertise and genre knowledge; point to the large proportion of published research written by multilingual scholars.

difficulties.pattern: 'Native norms are ideological, so I can ignore conventions.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Dismissal of feedback on genre conventions as native-speakerist.
difficulties.response: Distinguish genre conventions from nativeness and stress that choices to depart from conventions should be informed and deliberate.

difficulties.pattern: Treating first-language English peers as automatic authorities on academic writing.
difficulties.revealedBy: Group work in which drafting or editing is handed to first-language English members by default.
difficulties.response: Show that academic literacy is learned by all students and that genre knowledge, not nativeness, is the relevant expertise.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner whether a first-language English speaker automatically writes better academic English than a multilingual student.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Says no, explaining that academic literacy is learned and distinguishing genre knowledge from general proficiency.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Qualifies the claim but without a clear distinction.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Agrees without qualification.

guidance.contextNotes: Advanced pre-sessional and undergraduate learners can address the topic through feedback and group-work examples. PGT learners can examine institutional language policies; PGR learners engage most directly through publication, peer review and the politics of English-medium scholarship.
reviewNotes: EAP positions on how far to accommodate non-standard forms in assessed writing vary; this topic presents the debate rather than prescribing assessment policy.

authorNotes: arg.position overlaps ess.thesis-statement; I recommend ess.thesis-statement take arg.position (and arg.claim-types) as prerequisites, and that ess.* topics generally depend on ARG rather than the reverse. I have not linked any ARG topic to ess.* or ges.* topics.
arg.extended-argument overlaps ess.body-organisation; recommend ess.body-organisation take arg.extended-argument as a soft prerequisite.
arg.oral-argument overlaps sem.opinions and sem.debate; I linked sem.opinions as a prerequisite and recommend sem.debate take arg.oral-argument and arg.rebuttal-concession as prerequisites.

arg.evaluating-arguments and arg.argument-mapping depend on rdc.argument-identification and rdc.evidence-evaluation; RDC authors should not make those topics depend on arg.argument-mapping or arg.evaluating-arguments (cycle risk). rdc.argument-identification naturally takes arg.argument-concept as a prerequisite.
rdc.assumptions ('surfacing unstated premises') overlaps arg.warrants; recommend rdc.assumptions take arg.toulmin as a soft prerequisite rather than the reverse.
arg.exploratory-adversarial maps closely onto the ges.discussion-essay / ges.argumentative-essay distinction; recommend those genre topics take it as a soft prerequisite.
The skeleton name 'Claim types' uses the five-way rhetoric/composition taxonomy (stasis theory), whose bibliographic support is currently a proposed reference; walton2006 provides partial support.

crt.questioning overlaps heavily with rdc.critical-questions. I treat crt.questioning as the general habit and recommend that rdc.critical-questions take it as a soft prerequisite; I have not linked rdc.critical-questions into CRT to avoid a cycle.
crt.description-analysis-evaluation overlaps ess.criticality ('moving beyond description'); ess.criticality should take crt.description-analysis-evaluation as a prerequisite.
crt.reflexivity should be a prerequisite of res.positionality-writing, which is its genre-level realisation.
acu.disciplinary-knowledge overlaps crt.epistemic-beliefs; I recommend acu.disciplinary-knowledge take crt.epistemic-beliefs as a soft prerequisite (I have not linked in the other direction).

Gap: there is no topic for analogical reasoning (argument from analogy and precedent), which is central in law, history and policy writing; it could be absorbed into crt.reasoning-types or added as a separate topic.
Gap: there is no topic for ethical or normative reasoning (arguing from principles and consequences), which features in health, business, education and law assignments.

crt.problem-solving partly duplicates fun.problem-solution (language) and dbe.critical-frameworks (discipline tools); I have scoped it as the reasoning process and linked fun.problem-solution as a prerequisite.

idn.plurilingual-repertoire overlaps rdp.plurilingual-reading, wpr.l1-in-composing, src.multilingual-sources and dig.machine-translation. I treat it as the general strategic stance and recommend those topics take it as a soft prerequisite; I have not linked them as prerequisites of IDN topics to avoid cycles.

idn.intercultural-rhetoric overlaps coh.writer-responsibility, whose scope (Hinds's reader/writer responsibility) comes from contrastive rhetoric. Recommend coh.writer-responsibility take idn.intercultural-rhetoric as a soft prerequisite, or that its guidance avoid presenting reader/writer responsibility as a property of whole languages. I have not linked it to avoid a cycle.

idn.academic-identity overlaps sta.authorial-voice, sta.self-mention and gai.authorship-voice. I linked reg.impersonality-presence as a prerequisite, following the brief that register feeds identity; STA/REG authors should avoid making reg.impersonality-presence depend on anything downstream of idn.academic-identity. Recommend sta.authorial-voice take idn.academic-identity as a soft prerequisite.

Cycle-risk edges for the integrator: acu.transition, acu.academic-literacies and acu.discourse-communities are prerequisites of IDN topics; if ACU authors link IDN topics as prerequisites of these, one direction must be dropped.

idn.diversity-as-resource and idn.standards-legitimacy are as much curriculum principles for teachers as learner content, and overlap acu.critical-eap and pub.multilingual-scholars. Recommend pub.multilingual-scholars take idn.standards-legitimacy as a soft prerequisite.
The domain sits awkwardly in the 'Argument & Critical Thinking' strand; it might fit better under 'Academic Socialisation & Communication'. IDs are unaffected.
